_meta.purpose: Labelled eval set with per-lead keep/drop ground truth. Used by ../run_benchmark.py.
_meta.why_this_shape: Production sends up to 200 leads per call. Six leads is enough to encode every failure mode that matters (wrong seniority, wrong department, wrong geography, right-level-wrong-function) while keeping a full run cheap.

_vocabulary_source.how: Read from Oppora's live MCP endpoints get_available_management_levels and get_available_departments. Do NOT invent values here — a filter value production never sends is not a test, it is a fiction, and the model is graded on it anyway.
_vocabulary_source._fixed_2026_08_05: This file previously used 'VP' (Oppora's real value is 'Vice President') and 'Individual Contributor' (not a member of Oppora's taxonomy at all). Lead 102 became 'Entry' (SDR, 6 months in role) and lead 104 became 'Senior' (technician, 5 years, non-managerial). Both are still outside the VP/Director filters, so every keep/drop label and both cases' expected outcomes are unchanged — only the vocabulary is now real.
_vocabulary_source._api_quirk: get_available_management_levels returns 'Experienced  Manager' with a double space. Reproduced verbatim above for fidelity; avoid using that value in cases until it is confirmed to be intentional rather than a data-entry artefact.

score_leads_batch._fn: score_leads_batch(company_name, filters, leads, *, fallback_sets=None, total_required) -> LeadFilterResult
score_leads_batch._note: Each lead carries `_expect` = keep | drop | ambiguous. `ambiguous` rows are NOT scored for pass/fail — they exist to see how a model handles a partial match, which is where models differ most.

leads.name: Daniel Brooks
leads.title: Director of Sales
leads.headline: Director of Sales, East @ Notion
leads.summary: Runs the East Coast sales team out of the New York office.
leads._why: Second exact match. Its presence means total_required=2 has a single unambiguous correct answer: {101, 106}.

cases._scoring: keep-ids must appear in scored_leads; drop-ids must NOT. rank_and_select(total_required=2) must return exactly {101,106} as a set.

cases._why: Exercises the OTHER prompt branch — `fallback_sets` builds a PRIORITY LADDER and the model must assign priority_tier, not just a score. Same leads, so any behaviour change is attributable to the ladder alone.
cases._scoring: 101 must be tier 0 and 106 tier 1. 103/105 become acceptable at tier 2 under the ladder, so they are unscored. 102/104 match no tier and must still be dropped.

cases._why: Single-filter exact match. Baseline competence.

top_lead_generate_with_quality_check._note: Self-correcting loop: generate -> QA audit -> fix if score < 80 or not acceptable. 2 LLM calls on a pass, 3 on a fail. The model INVENTS the leads here (no input roster), so grading is structural, not factual — we cannot verify a hallucinated person exists.

cases.prompt: Recommend up to 2 leads at each of these companies for an AI SDR sales tool: Stripe, Notion. Prioritize VP/Director of Sales or Revenue Operations. For each lead set ai_recommendation to a short sentence on why they're a good fit, and use id=1, 2, 3... sequentially across the whole result.
cases._scoring: Structural only: right companies, <=2 leads each, ids 1..N with no gaps or repeats, every lead has a non-empty recommendation, and titles reflect the seniority asked for. `ids_sequential_from_1` is the interesting one — it is an explicit instruction most models drop when output spans multiple nested objects.
